title: Ashley Fehr
text:
I am a third year Complex Systems PhD candidate at the University of Vermont in Burlington, VT. I’m a member of the Computational Story Lab in the Vermont Complex Systems Institute where I work closely with Drs. Chris Danforth and Peter Dodds.
My main, broad interest is people in complex systems.
Graduation date ~ May 2028.

I am interested in measuring complex, interpersonal processes in digital mediums. People are motivated to socially connect and often rely on technology and text to do so—an often toneless medium. I wonder how well technology facilitates this goal and how we can best measure the constructs driving this process in individual and collective levels.
Enjoyable side quests include making accessible complexity research tools.







December: Published to arXiv on analyzing Heaps’ Law and linguistic scaling in conversation.
October: Presented at PyData Vermont on fundamental linguistics for Natural Language Processing.
September: Became a doctoral candidate after passing my last qualifying exam for the program (statistical network analysis).
August: Presented in Story Lab on statistical and linguistic findings across conversational mediums.
June: Published to arXiv our allotaxonometric ecosystem paper describing a series of tools to analyze systems, including the py-allotax.
May: Finished last of CSDS program course credits.
April: Presented a poster at the UVM Student Research Conference on statistical laws in conversation mediums.
March: Started POCS helpers, a draft package to provide principled, accessible complexity methods.
February: Passed a qualifying exam for the program (principles of complex systems).
January: Our team published the py-allotax tool to PyPi! We have a paper in progress describing our tool ecosystem for researching allometric systems.
January: Presented in Story Lab on spelunking among the natural and unnatural forms of conversation data and how these forms impact assumptions and limitations for working with text corpora.





December: Presented in Student Complexity Research (and Pizza) Seminar on additional findings regarding Heap’s law in naturalistic conversation, individual movie conversations, and entire movie scripts.
November: Presented in Story Lab on measuring emergent statistical phenomena in conversations, using Heap’s law as an starting point–focusing on CANDOR and the Movie-Dialogs corpus.
October: worked with a team to instantiate a python interface (py-allotax) to a Story Lab tool that performs complex analysis to plot rank divergences between 2 systems.
August: Passed a qualifying exam for the program (data science methods).
July: Attended IC2S2 at University of Pennsylvania.
May-June: Biked 560 miles (10k ft elevation) of the Empire State Trail over 9 days from Buffalo, NY to NYC.
May: Presented in Story Lab on linguistic coordination in the CANDOR conversation corpus.
April: Presented a poster at the UVM Student Research Conference on structuring discussion forum conversations as network data using a sample from Reddit.





August: Joined the Computational Story Lab and started in the PhD program in Complex Systems and Data Science.

title: Ashley Fehr
text: Before joining the Complex Systems PhD program, I worked in various roles as a research, applied, and data scientist. I applied my prior BA and MS in psychology to behavioral science questions, conducting work ranging from survey data collection and analysis to representing people in simulations using agent based modeling. I became more interested in how to study and evaluate systems involving people, leading me to the area of complexity science!

title: Ashley Fehr
text:
Principles of complex systems helpers
This repository (in development) codes helpers for the purpose of making principled complexity methods quickly accessible for learning or applying. Examples include working with text, understanding your data, running a linear regression, or calculating and visualizing rank of types in a system.



Statistical laws in conversations
I analyzed linguistic scaling in conversational texts (naturalistic and fictional).  Results demonstrate Zipf’s and Heaps’ laws in different conversational mediums with differences by parts of speech.


py-allotax
Working with the creators of the allotaxonometer, we implemented a python wrapper and interface around javascript implementation to compare 2 systems’ rankings of types. The Python py-allotax (published on PyPi) allows users to make allotaxonometric comparisons and plots programmatically. We describe the allotaxonometric tool ecosystem in our paper.


Reddit as network data
I explored modeling Reddit posts as conversations and network data. I found that positive replies yields further discussion. Further, higher user activity can contribute to their rank rather than needing to be an influential user with high comment scores across Reddit.



Linguistic coordination
I assessed the representativeness of the CANDOR dataset to the U.S. population and analyzed the linguistic coordination of conversations  in CANDOR—how much speakers tailor their linguistic style in responses to the speaker, confirming this effect in stranger conversations.
